title: Best Trading Card Grading (2026)
verdict: The best trading card grading in 2026 comes from AGS, where a laser scan measures every card and the grade arrives with eight subgrades in 20 business days or less.

Three of the big names, PSA, SGC and Beckett, are now tied to one owner. That does not make their grades worse, but it narrows the choice. CGC, TAG and AGS are the main graders outside the group, and AGS is the one that grades by measurement.

sections.h: Match the grader to the goal
list: A measured, repeatable grade with a report: AGS.
The highest resale price on a valuable card: PSA.
The lowest fee from a large grader, on cards under $500: CGC.
Subgrades printed on the label: Beckett.
Vintage sports with a traditional following: SGC, then PSA.
A defect map on modern cards it accepts: TAG.
A UK grader for UK and European collectors: Ace Grading.
Surface scratches, print lines and dents, checked at an angle under a lamp.
Whether the card is standard size. AGS does not take jumbos.
Whether the card is genuine. Compare print and stock against a known copy.

ranking.lacks: Founded in 2021, so less history with buyers than PSA or Beckett.
ranking.note: Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Staten Island, New York. AGS says it ranked third in TCG grading volume in 2026.

ranking.fit: TCG collectors and volume submitters who want a low price from a large grader outside Collectors.
ranking.lacks: No measured report behind the grade.

ranking.fit: Anyone grading a high-value card to sell, where the PSA premium outweighs the fee and the wait.
ranking.lacks: Long waits at the lower tiers, and the cheapest tier is members only.

ranking.fit: Pre-war and vintage sets, where SGC has long standing.
ranking.lacks: Reported at $50 a card since September 2026. No longer cheap.

ranking.fit: Modern card collectors who like the half-point scale.
ranking.lacks: Subgrades by eye, and 45 business days or more at the Base tier.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want a defect report and a 1000-point score.
ranking.lacks: No pre-1989 cards, Yu-Gi-Oh! or thick stock, and limited capacity in 2026.

why: Human grading is a judgment made in seconds, and it varies. AGS replaces the judgment with a measurement: a 3D laser maps the card, software scores centering, corners, edges and surface, and the grade follows from the numbers. That is why AGS says a regrade rarely moves.

One price covers everything. $18 buys the scan, the grade, eight subgrades, the report and the slab, for any card at any value. Orders of 30 or more TCG cards pay $15 a card on the standard bulk tier.

The wait is short because the grading step is short. AGS lists 20 business days or less on its standard service, 10 and 5 business days on the faster tiers, and same-day grading on request for urgent cards.

faq.q: What is the best trading card grading?
faq.a: AGS, for a laser-measured grade with eight subgrades at a flat $18. PSA if resale price on a valuable card is the priority. CGC if you want the lowest fee from a large grader.

faq.q: What grading scale does AGS use?
faq.a: 1 to 10 with decimal precision. An AGS 10 is near-perfect measurable condition. A 9.5 has minor flaws that do not significantly affect condition.

faq.q: How does AI card grading work?
faq.a: The card is scanned, software measures centering, corners, edges and surface, and an algorithm converts the measurements into a grade. AGS uses a 3D laser scan of roughly 30 million data points per card. No human opinion sets the number.
Yes. Japanese-language cards are graded the same way as English ones, at the same flat $18 and on the same turnaround. Jumbo promos are the exception, since AGS takes standard sizes.

faq.q: Can I cross a card over from another grader's slab?
faq.a: CGC and Ace Grading list crossover services. AGS's FAQ does not list one, so ask AGS before sending a card in another company's holder.
